analysis.one_liner: Bans surprise credit card rate hikes, universal default, and many card fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for credit cards: card issuers would have to give 45 days' notice before raising an interest rate, could not raise rates because of a late payment on some other debt (universal default), could not charge interest on amounts paid within the grace period, and would face new limits on over-the-limit, late, and other fees. It would also require payments to be applied to the highest-interest balance first, and would restrict issuing credit cards to people under 21 unless they had a co-signer, showed income, or completed a financial literacy course. The bill never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit cardholders, especially the tens of millions who carry a balance. The bill targeted practices that raised cardholders' rates without warning, charged fees on top of fees, and applied payments in ways that maximized interest charges. It also gave special attention to students and young adults, a heavily marketed group.

how_it_helps.text: Card issuers would have to give 45 days' advance notice before raising an interest rate, could not apply the increase to existing balances, and would have to explain cardholders' right to cancel the account before the increase takes effect.

The bill would prohibit universal default — raising a cardholder's rate based on unrelated information like a credit score or a late payment on a different account — and would bar issuers from changing card terms unilaterally before renewal.

It would ban interest charges on balances repaid within the grace period, prohibit interest on fees, restrict over-the-limit fees to one per billing cycle (with a consumer option to have over-limit transactions declined instead of fee'd), cap fees that exceed the issuer's actual cost, and bar separate fees just to pay a bill.

Payments would have to be applied to the highest-interest balance first, billing cycles would run at least 21 days, and statements would have to show how long — and at what total cost — paying only the minimum would take to pay off the balance.

People under 21 could not get a card without a co-signer, proof of independent income, or a certified financial literacy course, and universities could not market affinity cards to them without those requirements met.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, whose fee and interest income the bill directly curtailed. Some cost could trickle to cardholders if issuers responded by charging higher upfront rates or annual fees, or by offering less credit to weaker borrowers.

drawbacks.text: The bill would restrict credit access for adults under 21, who could only get a card with a co-signer, proof of independent repayment ability, or a completed financial literacy course — a genuine tradeoff for young adults who build credit early.

By banning penalty pricing and universal default, the bill would push issuers to charge all borrowers higher upfront rates rather than repricing risky borrowers later, a cost that would land partly on cardholders who never trigger penalties.
Reasonableness standards for fees and currency-exchange charges would require case-by-case regulatory judgment, which issuers argued invites litigation and compliance costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections aimed at practices that regulators and the Federal Reserve had already flagged as deceptive — surprise rate increases on old balances, universal default, and fees stacked on fees — and the direct cost fell on issuer revenue rather than on taxpayers. The main honest objections are the under-21 access restriction and the likelihood that some costs would be repriced into higher rates for everyone, but the design was strongly consumer-protective. The bill never got a hearing, so none of these tradeoffs were ever tested in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the Credit CARD Act of 2008 on July 10, 2008, with 12 original co-sponsors including Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, and John Kerry.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction.
Sixteen senators co-sponsored the bill — 15 Democrats and one Independent — and no further action was taken on it for the rest of the 110th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, which kept the rate-increase, universal-default, and fee practices the bill would have banned throughout the 110th Congress. Cardholders got none of the protections, though a substantially similar law passed the next Congress in 2009.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit CARD Act of 2008 and delivered introductory remarks in the Senate.

for.name: 16 senators (15 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Co-sponsored the bill, including Sens. Levin, Menendez, Sanders, Obama, and Clinton.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; referred the bill on introduction
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 10, 2008 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banks
against.what_they_did: The industry lobbied heavily against restrictions on rate increases, universal default, and penalty fees as similar legislation moved in this period; that pressure does not appear in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and co-sponsors were Democratic-caucus senators (15 Democrats and one Independent, Bernie Sanders); no Republican co-sponsored, and the bill never reached a roll-call vote.

industries.note: The bill would have directly cut issuer revenue from universal default rate hikes, retroactive rate increases, over-limit and late fees, interest charged on fee amounts, and payment-application practices that maximized interest. Cardholders' gain was the issuers' loss by design.
Title III would restrict affinity card agreements between issuers and institutions of higher education, ending lucrative campus marketing deals aimed at students under 21.

The bill would only require a Government Accountability Office study of interchange fees — the fees merchants pay on card transactions — and how they are disclosed and overseen, with no substantive mandate in this bill.
